Baptized
bap-TIZED
v. (past part.)
From Greek baptizo, to dip, to immerse, to plunge; the intensive of bapto, to dip. Webster 1828: administered the sacrament of baptism to; christened. The Greek word was ordinary before it was ecclesiastical — used of dyeing cloth by dipping and of a ship sunk in the sea.

Biblical Definition

Baptized describes what was done to every believer in the book of Acts, and the New Testament never pictures an unbaptized Christian. The order is fixed: the word is heard, the word is received, and the receivers are baptized. Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls (Acts 2:41). Gladly receiving precedes the water; nothing in the sentence permits reversal. The Lord Himself submitted to it as the opening act of His public ministry: And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water (Matthew 3:16) — out of the water, which is the plain description of a man who had been in it. Paul makes the mode the picture of the meaning: Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? (Romans 6:3). Burial and rising are the figure, and immersion is the only mode that shows it. And the outward act signifies an inward and Spirit-wrought union: For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free (1 Corinthians 12:13). The sign does not create the union; it declares it, and the church receives the one baptized as a member of the body Christ purchased.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BAPTIZED as having received the ordinance of baptism; christened. Webster’s entry for the verb notes that the Greek word signifies to dip or immerse, and that the practice of the primitive church was immersion, sprinkling and pouring having been introduced later.

expand to see more

BAPTIZED, pp. — Having received the ordinance of baptism; initiated by water into the visible church.

The Greek baptizo signifies properly to dip, to plunge, to immerse; and this was the practice of the primitive church.

Figuratively, overwhelmed or immersed in suffering; as, the baptism of blood which Christ endured.

Applied also to the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the church, called the baptism of the Holy Ghost.

From Greek bapto, to dip — the root also of baptism, Baptist, and baptistery.

Key Scripture

Acts 2:41 — "Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls."

Matthew 3:16 — "And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:"

Romans 6:3 — "Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death?"

1 Corinthians 12:13 — "For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit."

Modern Corruption

Baptismal regeneration makes the water do what only the Spirit does, and paedobaptism reverses the New Testament order by administering the sign to those who have not yet gladly received the word.

expand to see more

Baptismal regeneration — held by Rome, by the Eastern churches, and in varying strength by Lutheran and Anglican sacramental theology — teaches that the water conveys the new birth rather than signifying it. Acts 2:41 forbids this at the level of grammar: they gladly received the word, and then were baptized. Simon Magus in Acts 8 was baptized and remained in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity, which settles the question by counter-example. The sign seals a reality already given; a seal on an empty deed conveys nothing, and the pastoral damage of teaching otherwise is a congregation of the baptized-and-unconverted who have been told the decisive thing already happened to them in infancy.

Paedobaptism is the graver error among Reformed brethren precisely because so much else in their theology is sound, and the dictionary names it as error rather than difference. The argument runs from circumcision as the covenant sign given to infants, but the New Covenant is expressly the covenant in which they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest (Hebrews 8:11) — a covenant without an unregenerate membership. Every baptism recorded in Acts follows a credible profession, and Romans 6:3 defines the act as a burial into Christ’s death, which cannot be predicated of an infant who has not died with Him. The 1689 Confession states the Baptist position plainly and the dictionary holds it: the subjects are those who actually profess repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, and the mode is immersion.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek baptizo (G907), to immerse, to submerge; baptisma (G908), the act of immersion; bapto (G911), to dip; Hebrew tabal (H2881), to dip, used of Naaman dipping seven times in Jordan.

expand to see more

Greek baptizo (G907) — to dip repeatedly, to immerge, to submerge; the ordinary word for sinking a vessel or dyeing cloth.

Greek baptisma (G908) — the ordinance itself; the New Testament coined this noun for the Christian rite.

Greek bapto (G911) — the simple verb, to dip; dip the tip of his finger in water (Luke 16:24).

Hebrew tabal (H2881) — to dip; Naaman dipped himself seven times in Jordan (2 Kings 5:14), the Old Testament picture of cleansing by immersion.

Greek louo (G3068) and nipto (G3538) — to wash the whole body and to wash a part; the New Testament keeps these distinct from baptizo.

Usage

"They that gladly received his word were baptized (Acts 2:41) — the fixed New Testament order of profession before water."

"Went up straightway out of the water (Matthew 3:16) — the Lord’s own baptism describing the mode."

"Baptized into his death (Romans 6:3) — the meaning the mode was chosen to picture."
